enonce_markdown: A school bursar has the monthly budget of the Parents' Association for one term: rent, salaries, water and electricity, repairs and stationery. She wants a chart that shows what share of the total budget each of these five categories takes. Which chart type is the most suitable?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Choose the chart type from the question being asked: parts of a whole -> pie; trend over time -> line; comparison of values -> column or bar; relationship between two numbers -> scatter.

### Solution

The question concerns the **share of each category in a single total**, so each category must be drawn as a slice of one circle: a **pie chart**. A line chart suggests an order or a trend over time, which categories do not have; a scatter chart needs two numeric variables; a surface chart shows three numeric dimensions.

choix.texte: A line chart, with one point per category
An XY (scatter) chart, with categories on both axes
A pie chart, with one slice per category
A surface chart, with one layer per category

enonce_markdown: A column chart shows the number of computers sold by three shops (Douala, Bamenda, Garoua) in each quarter. The chart has no text other than the bars. State **two** chart elements that must be added so that a reader can understand it, and explain the purpose of each.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A chart must say what it shows (title), what each axis measures (axis titles and units) and which colour means which series (legend).

### Solution

Any two of the following, each with its purpose:

- **Chart title**, e.g. *Computers sold per quarter*: tells the reader what the chart is about.
- **Axis titles**: the horizontal axis labelled *Quarter* and the vertical axis labelled *Number of computers sold*, so the reader knows what is measured and in which unit.
- **Legend**: shows which colour of column belongs to Douala, Bamenda or Garoua; without it the three series cannot be told apart.
- **Data labels** (optional): print the exact value on each column so that it can be read without estimating from the gridlines.

enonce_markdown: The monthly sales of two shops, Shop A and Shop B, are stored in a worksheet for January to June (months in column A, Shop A in column B, Shop B in column C). The owner wants to compare how the sales of the two shops **evolve over the six months**. Which chart is the most appropriate?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

To compare how several series change over ordered categories such as time, plot all series in one line (or clustered column) chart with the time on the category axis.

### Solution

The aim is a **comparison of trends over time for two series**. A line chart with the months as categories and two series (B and C) draws both evolutions on the same axes, so they can be compared directly. A pie chart shows shares of one total and cannot show evolution; the two single-pie options also hide either one shop or the months. The scatter option puts text (shop names) on an axis meant for numbers and reverses the roles of the variables.

choix.texte: A line chart with the months on the horizontal axis and one line (series) for each shop
A pie chart with one slice for each month, using the sales of Shop A only
A pie chart for each shop, using only its total sales for the six months
An XY (scatter) chart with the shop names on the horizontal axis and the months on the vertical axis

enonce_markdown: In a worksheet, column A contains the names of 5 students, column B their age and column C their ICT test mark. You want a chart of the **marks** against the **names**, without the ages. What must you do before inserting the chart?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Non-adjacent ranges are selected by holding Ctrl while selecting the second range; Shift extends a selection into one continuous block.

### Solution

The two needed columns (A and C) are not next to each other. Select A1:A6 (headings included), keep **Ctrl** pressed and select C1:C6: both ranges are then chosen and the chart uses A for the categories and C for the values. With **Shift**, or by dragging over A1:C6, the selection becomes one block that also contains column B, so the ages would be plotted as a second series. Selecting only C1:C6 gives a chart whose categories are 1, 2, 3... instead of the student names.

choix.texte: Select A1:A6, hold the Shift key, then select C1:C6
Select A1:A6, hold the Ctrl key, then select C1:C6

enonce_markdown:
The sales table below was used to draw a column chart, but the person selected all the rows, including the last one.

| Month | Sales (FCFA thousand) |
|---|---|
| Jan | 1200 |
| Feb | 1500 |
| Mar | 1350 |
| Apr | 1800 |
| May | 1650 |
| Jun | 1500 |
| TOTAL | 9000 |

Explain what is wrong with the resulting chart and state how to correct it. Give the ratio of the TOTAL column to the largest monthly column.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A chart should plot only values of the same kind and scale; a totals row is a summary of the other rows and must be left out of the selection.

### Solution

The TOTAL row is selected as if it were a seventh month. Its value is 9000, while the largest month is 1800, so the TOTAL column is 9000/1800 = 5 times as high as the tallest month.

- The vertical axis scale is stretched up to about 10 000 so the six monthly columns are squashed and their differences become hard to see.
- The chart is also misleading, since the total is not a month.

**Correction:** reselect only the heading and the six month rows (rows Jan to Jun), leaving out the TOTAL row, or edit the data range of the chart with *Select Data* so that the last row is removed. If the total is needed, show it in a separate cell or a separate chart.

enonce_markdown: A table gives the marks of three schools (rows: Kumba, Yaounde, Buea) in four subjects (columns: Maths, Physics, Chemistry, Biology). A clustered column chart is to be drawn so that the subjects are grouped along the horizontal axis and, within each group, there is one coloured column for each school. Which description of the finished chart is correct, and what must be done if the first chart shows the opposite arrangement?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In a clustered column chart each series (one legend entry) gives one column in every group of the category axis; the number of columns is series x categories.

### Solution

Categories along the horizontal axis = the 4 subjects, so there are **4 groups**. Series = the schools, one colour each, so the legend has **3 entries**. Each group contains one column per school, so the chart has $3 \times 4 = 12$ columns. If Excel has made the schools the categories (the opposite arrangement), use *Chart Design > Switch Row/Column*, which exchanges the roles of rows and columns without changing the data. A stacked column would change how the columns are drawn, not which data are grouped, and 7 is just 3 + 4, the number of headings, not the number of columns.

choix.texte: 4 legend entries, 3 groups of columns, 12 columns in all; use Switch Row/Column if the groups are the schools
3 legend entries, 4 groups of columns, 12 columns in all; use Switch Row/Column if the groups are the schools
3 legend entries, 4 groups of columns, 7 columns in all; change the chart to a stacked column
7 legend entries, 12 groups of columns, 3 columns in all; retype the table with the subjects as rows only
